title: TransXplainRRG: A Radiologist-Evaluated LVLM for Chest Radiograph Report Generation
authors: Chayan Mondal, Duc-Son Pham, Tele Tan, Ashu Gupta, Vincent T. Y. Tiong, Shreya Ghosh
abstract: Recent advancements in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLM) enhance X-ray report generation, but often neglect clinical context, overlook workflow integration, and lack explainability, which hinders clinical adoption due to interpretability and reliability concerns. This paper addresses the dual challenges of performance and expert explainability in automated X-ray report generation for clinical AI applications. Our proposed approach, TransXplainRRG, utilises an off-the-shelf Swin Transformer model along with a transformer-based text encoder that incorporates patient medical history to generate a radiology report. Further, we explore an expert-guided `inside-out' approach and extract only abnormal findings for radiology report refinement. Thus, this study bridges the gap between high-performance automation and interpretability critical for clinical practice by combining state-of-the-art transformer-based vision encoders, text encoders, and LLMs. TransXplainRRG is trained and tested on the large-scale MIMIC-CXR dataset and further evaluated on the unseen IU X-Ray dataset to demonstrate its generalizability and robustness. We employed the GREEN metric as a complementary measure of clinical consistency, achieving scores of 0.327 on MIMIC-CXR and 0.605 on IU X-Ray, both higher than those achieved by MAIRA-2 under the same evaluation setting. It also performed competitively across standard evaluation metrics, frequently matching or surpassing state-of-the-art models. Additionally, we introduce qualitative evaluation metrics developed from radiologists' viewpoints and conduct a preliminary radiologist evaluation on 100 generated reports to assess their clinical relevance. Quantitative and qualitative analyses further demonstrate the potential of our TransXplainRRG framework for reliable and explainable radiology report generation.

infographic.key_insight: TransXplainRRG combines chest X-ray images, patient history, and expert-guided report refinement, achieving higher GREEN clinical-consistency scores than MAIRA-2 in the reported evaluation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework aims to make automated chest radiograph reports more clinically relevant and interpretable, but clinical deployment readiness is not established.
method: Encode X-ray images with a Swin Transformer and patient history with a transformer-based text encoder.
Generate reports using a vision-language framework.
Apply expert-guided “inside-out” analysis and abnormal-finding extraction to refine reports.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained and tested on MIMIC-CXR and evaluated on unseen IU X-Ray data, the model achieved GREEN scores of 0.327 and 0.605, respectively; radiologists also preliminarily evaluated 100 generated reports.
infographic.watch_item: The preliminary 100-report radiologist evaluation does not establish safety or effectiveness in routine clinical workflows.
infographic.paper_title: TransXplainRRG: A Radiologist-Evaluated LVLM for Chest Radiograph Report Generation

title: Curiosity-0826-4B: Generative Medical Event Sequence Modeling Across Pediatric and Adult Populations
authors: Mani Nagarathnam, Luke Benham, Paul Blazek, John Cashy, Kevin Chung, John Muenning
abstract: We introduce Curiosity-0826-4B, an updated version of the generative medical event foundation model trained on Epic Cosmos that simulates patient timelines to produce zero-shot clinical predictions. Curiosity-0826-4B incorporates a broader patient population and richer clinical event representations, while generally matching or exceeding Curiosity-0226-1B, the largest model in the previous Curiosity-0226 series, on evaluated tasks supported by both models. Laboratory value prediction improved, with MAE 18--46% lower than that of Curiosity-0226-1B. We evaluated prediction of disease events across pediatric cohorts aged 2--17 years. AUROCs for new asthma diagnosis (0.742--0.785) and asthma exacerbation (0.829--0.852) were comparable to those in the adult reference cohort, while AUROCs for sickle cell crisis (0.820--0.847) were lower than in adults (0.915). Explicit representation of documented death enabled new mortality prediction tasks among adults across hospice, inpatient, and ambulatory settings (AUROC 0.821--0.942). Scaling-law analysis guided compute-optimal initial pretraining followed by continued pretraining with context extension. The resulting Curiosity-0826-4B model has more parameters (4.3B versus 1B) and a longer context window (16K versus 8K). It processes 56% fewer training tokens and requires 2.2 times the training floating point operations (FLOPs) compared with its predecessor. By extending a common zero-shot prediction strategy to pediatric patients and additional outcomes, Curiosity-0826-4B broadens opportunities to develop clinical and operational applications without training separate task-specific models. Further validation should assess local calibration, performance across patient subgroups and event frequencies, timeline completion rates, and generalization to new settings, alongside prospective evaluation of clinical and operational utility.

infographic.key_insight: Curiosity-0826-4B broadens zero-shot medical event prediction to pediatric patients and adult mortality while reducing laboratory prediction error by 18–46% versus its predecessor.
infographic.clinical_relevance: A shared model could support prediction across multiple clinical outcomes without separate task-specific training, but clinical utility remains unproven.
method: Generative model trained on Epic Cosmos to simulate patient timelines.
Expanded population coverage and richer clinical event representations, including documented death.
Scaling-guided pretraining produced a 4.3B-parameter model with a 16K context window.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations reported AUROCs of 0.742–0.785 for pediatric asthma diagnosis, 0.829–0.852 for pediatric asthma exacerbation, 0.820–0.847 for pediatric sickle cell crisis, and 0.821–0.942 for adult mortality.
infographic.watch_item: Local calibration, subgroup performance, generalization to new settings, and prospective clinical utility require further validation before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Curiosity-0826-4B: Generative Medical Event Sequence Modeling Across Pediatric and Adult Populations

title: Fine-Tuned Small Language Model for Synthetic Clinical Data Generation and Predictive Healthcare Analytics
authors: Mihnea Sebastian Burlacu, Ionut Anghel, Tudor Cioara
abstract: The reduced availability of medical datasets represents an important challenge in the development of predictive models for remote healthcare solutions, especially when the available data are imbalanced or difficult to extend through traditional methods. Small Language Models (SLMs) have become a promising alternative to Large Language Models (LLMs) for addressing these limitations due to their lower computational requirements and adaptability to specialized tasks. However, their performance remains highly dependent on the quality and representativeness of the available training data. In this paper, we propose a method for clinical data augmentation based on a fine-tuned Microsoft Phi-2 model that is used to generate synthetic instances, with the purpose of improving deep learning-based model for predicting remotely monitored vital signs. The Phi-2 model was adapted to the medical domain through supervised fine-tuning on the MedQuad dataset, through a Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA)-based method and by applying few-shot prompting techniques. The resulting model was used afterwards in the augmentation of a small-sized dataset, composed of vital sign values and labels associated with pathological and physiological states. The experimental results demonstrate that fine-tuned SLMs improved the performance on medical domain, achieving higher scores for both lexical (ROUGE) and semantic (BERTScore) evaluation metrics compared to the pretrained model. Moreover, the fine-tuned SLM is effective for generating structured synthetic clinical data. When used for data augmentation, the generated dataset improved the performance of a LSTM predictive model, increasing the classification accuracy from 89.0% to 93.7% and showing consistent improvements in precision, recall, and F1-score.

infographic.key_insight: Synthetic clinical data generated by a fine-tuned Phi-2 model improved an LSTM classifier’s accuracy from 89.0% to 93.7% in the reported experiment.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could support predictive modeling for remote vital-sign monitoring when labeled clinical datasets are small or imbalanced.
method: Adapted Microsoft Phi-2 to medical content using MedQuad and supervised QLoRA fine-tuning.
Used few-shot prompting to generate structured synthetic vital-sign records with physiological and pathological labels.
Augmented a small dataset and evaluated downstream LSTM classification performance.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports higher ROUGE and BERTScore than pretrained Phi-2, alongside improved downstream accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report dataset size or external validation, leaving generalizability and clinical deployment readiness uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Fine-Tuned Small Language Model for Synthetic Clinical Data Generation and Predictive Healthcare Analytics

title: A frontier machine intelligence for human neuroimaging
authors: Chenhui Zhao, Akshay Rao, Akhil Kondepudi, Yiwei Lyu, Xinhai Hou, Rikhil Seshadri
abstract: Medical imaging is essential for diagnosing disease, guiding treatment and monitoring patients over time. Although artificial intelligence has advanced image interpretation, existing medical models often address restricted tasks, while general-purpose proprietary models lack access to private clinical imaging required to achieve medical expertise. Developing models that can interpret complex examinations and communicate their findings in the context of clinical decisions remains a major challenge. Here, we show that Neuro-VL, a vision-language model trained on nearly one million neuroimaging studies from routine clinical care, can interpret complete imaging examinations and engage in natural language conversations about their findings. Across internal and international datasets, Neuro-VL outperformed frontier general-purpose and specialized medical models in diagnosing, localizing, and describing abnormalities, as well as generating comprehensive radiology reports. The model also compared serial examinations to assess disease progression and more reliably resisted misleading clinical assumptions than leading frontier models from OpenAI and Google. These results extend health system learning beyond individual predictions to interactive image interpretation and longitudinal disease monitoring. They demonstrate how the collective clinical experience of health systems can be used to develop medical AI with specialized expertise and broad clinical capabilities.

infographic.key_insight: Neuro-VL is a specialized vision-language model that interprets complete neuroimaging examinations and discusses findings in natural language.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Its reported capabilities could support radiology reporting and assessment of disease progression, but do not establish readiness for clinical deployment.
method: Trained on nearly one million neuroimaging studies from routine clinical care.
Evaluated abnormality diagnosis, localization, description and comprehensive report generation.
Compared serial examinations and tested resistance to misleading clinical assumptions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across internal and international datasets, the abstract reports stronger performance than general-purpose and specialized medical models, without providing numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Prospective clinical validation is needed to establish safety and reliability before routine use.
infographic.paper_title: A frontier machine intelligence for human neuroimaging

title: Capacity-Constrained Delayed Feedback for Online Conformal Risk Control
authors: Bowen Wang, Osvaldo Simeone
abstract: Online conformal risk control (OCRC) enables reliable uncertainty quantification in machine learning by converting model outputs into prediction sets with long-term risk guarantees. These guarantees, however, hinge on the assumption that the loss of each round is revealed immediately and losslessly. In practice, feedback may be delayed, and limited resources may prevent tracking all pending predictions, causing some feedback to be lost. To address this challenge, we develop capacity-aware OCRC (CA-OCRC), a framework that jointly determines how to allocate limited tracking feedback capacity and how to construct prediction sets. CA-OCRC is based on a randomized tracking policy that samples a proxy delay to decide whether, and for how long, feedback for the current round is tracked. CA-OCRC updates the prediction sets via inverse probability weighting, compensating for the possibility of feedback lost due to delays and limited tracking capacity. We analyze risk bounds for both arbitrary and stochastic delays, revealing a trade-off between receiving more feedback and avoiding capacity saturation. Building on these bounds, we optimize the proxy delay distribution, showing scaling laws for the tracking capacity that ensure the same long-term risk as OCRC with unlimited feedback. Experiments on medical imaging, natural language processing, computer vision, and wireless communications show the effectiveness of CA-OCRC as compared to existing OCRC mechanisms.

infographic.key_insight: Capacity-aware online conformal risk control (CA-OCRC) adapts prediction sets when delayed feedback and limited tracking capacity cause some outcomes to be missed.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For medical imaging AI, this approach could support uncertainty estimation when outcome feedback arrives late and only a limited number of predictions can be tracked.
method: Randomly samples a proxy delay to decide whether and how long to track each prediction.
Uses inverse probability weighting to account for feedback lost through delays or capacity limits.
Optimizes tracking policies using risk bounds for arbitrary and stochastic delays.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports experiments across medical imaging, natural language processing, computer vision, and wireless communications, but provides no dataset details or numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Clinical benefit is not established by the abstract, and implementation requires balancing feedback collection against tracking-capacity saturation.
infographic.paper_title: Capacity-Constrained Delayed Feedback for Online Conformal Risk Control

title: Evaluating Pretrained Language Semantics for Structured EHR Prediction Tasks
authors: Ashvin Gupta, Brendan Delaney, Alessandra Russo
abstract: Structured Electronic Health Records (EHR) models typically treat each clinical concept as a dataset-specific token, discarding the natural-language semantics associated with the event. As a result, relationships between concepts must largely be learned from EHR co-occurrence, without directly exploiting any prior semantic knowledge. We investigate how pretrained causal language models can be adapted for longitudinal EHR prediction by developing tEHR. Here, we represent events with their natural language description and use this text stream to apply EHR-adaptive continued pretraining, followed by task-specific discriminative fine-tuning using LoRA, utilising the LLM as a longitudinal patient-encoder. We evaluate this approach across four prediction tasks on the MIMIC-IV dataset and pancreatic cancer prediction on the CPRD dataset at 1 to 12 month horizons, with tEHR using the Mistral-7B-v0.3 backbone achieving the strongest overall performance. Ablations show that performance declines when clinical descriptions are removed or misaligned, when numerical values are omitted, and when either stage of adaptation is removed, while explicit elapsed-time descriptions provide little additional benefit. Analysis of the learned patient representations further reveals clinically coherent structure associated with distinct patterns of disease risk and clinical history.

infographic.key_insight: tEHR uses pretrained language semantics to model structured patient histories, with meaningful clinical descriptions and two-stage adaptation contributing to prediction performance.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could support EHR-based risk prediction by leveraging the meanings of clinical events rather than treating them only as dataset-specific tokens.
method: Represent longitudinal EHR events using natural-language descriptions and numerical values.
Continue pretraining a causal language model on EHR text streams.
Apply task-specific discriminative fine-tuning with LoRA to predict outcomes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covered four MIMIC-IV prediction tasks and CPRD pancreatic cancer prediction at 1–12-month horizons; the Mistral-7B-v0.3 backbone performed strongest overall.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish prospective clinical utility or generalizability beyond the evaluated datasets.
infographic.paper_title: Evaluating Pretrained Language Semantics for Structured EHR Prediction Tasks

title: KQML-Liver: Interpretable Hybrid Quantum Machine Learning with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Liver Disease Classification
authors: Nhat-Long Nguyen, Viet-Loi Dinh, Trong-Nghia Pham
abstract: Liver disease remains a major global health concern, highlighting the need for reliable and accessible early detection methods. Although recent advances in machine learning, deep learning and quantum machine learning (QML) have introduced promising diagnostic tools, many approaches suffer from limited interpretability and inflated performance caused by data leakage or overly simplistic evaluation protocols. These constraints reduce their reliability in real-world clinical practice. This paper proposes KQML-Liver, a hybrid framework that integrates QML with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) to enhance predictive performance and interpretability. The architecture combines parameterized quantum circuits for expressive feature representation with KAN-based functional mappings that capture nonlinear relationships in an interpretable manner. Evaluated on the Indian Liver Patient Dataset (ILPD) under a rigorous preprocessing protocol preventing data leakage, the proposed model achieves 82% classification accuracy and 100% recall, detecting all positive cases, outperforming existing baselines while providing improved transparency in clinical predictions. These results suggest that hybrid KAN-quantum architectures offer a promising direction for interpretable AI-assisted medical diagnosis.

infographic.key_insight: KQML-Liver combines quantum machine learning with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, reporting 82% accuracy and 100% recall for liver disease classification.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could support interpretable liver disease detection, but clinical usefulness remains unestablished.
method: Parameterized quantum circuits represent input features.
Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks model nonlinear relationships through interpretable functional mappings.
Preprocessing is designed to prevent data leakage.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on the Indian Liver Patient Dataset reported 82% accuracy and detection of all positive cases; the abstract does not specify evaluation sample size or uncertainty.
infographic.watch_item: External validation and specificity reporting are needed to assess generalizability and false-positive burden.
infographic.paper_title: KQML-Liver: Interpretable Hybrid Quantum Machine Learning with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Liver Disease Classification

title: A thorough review on Deep Learning approaches to 2D-to-3D Registration in Medical Imaging
authors: Andrea Borghesi, Julia van Beurden, Maarten van Alphen, Michiel van den Brekel, Luc Karssemakers, Jan-Jakob Sonke
abstract: 2D-to-3D image registration is a key component for several medical imaging purposes such as intraoperative guidance, enabling the alignment between preoperative 3D volumes and real-time 2D images. While conventional optimisation-based methods often struggle with non-convex objectives, sensitivity to initialisation, and high computational demands, deep learning (DL) has emerged as a promising alternative, offering improved alignment robustness and the potential for real-time performance. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of DL frameworks developed to address the challenges inherent in 2D-to-3D registration. We first outline how core concepts of DL are adapted to the registration problem. We then examine recent methodological advancements from multiple perspectives, including pipeline design, architectural innovations, and domain adaptation strategies. Particular attention is given to quantitative metrics, highlighting how performance is defined and measured across studies. Across the 41 included studies, we find that direct regression is the most common pipeline (23 studies, against 18 iterative ones), that hybrid CNN-attention architectures are gaining ground, and that research remains heavily concentrated on X-ray-to-CT registration. We conclude by identifying the absence of per-case uncertainty estimation and the strong neglect of temporal or sequential modelling as the two methodological gaps most consequential for clinical readiness, and discuss state-space models as a way to add temporal memory within intraoperative latency budgets. Further opportunities lie in more principled domain adaptation and in the integration of foundation models for representation learning.

infographic.key_insight: This review finds that deep learning offers promising 2D-to-3D image alignment, but uncertainty estimation and temporal modelling remain key gaps for clinical readiness.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Aligning preoperative 3D volumes with real-time 2D images could support intraoperative guidance.
method: Reviews deep learning pipeline designs and architectures for 2D-to-3D registration.
Examines domain adaptation strategies and quantitative performance metrics.
Identifies opportunities for temporal memory and foundation-model representations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 41 reviewed studies, 23 used direct regression and 18 used iterative pipelines, with research concentrated on X-ray-to-CT registration.
infographic.watch_item: The reported absence of per-case uncertainty estimation limits assessment of alignment reliability in individual cases.
infographic.paper_title: A thorough review on Deep Learning approaches to 2D-to-3D Registration in Medical Imaging

title: Hx2Dx: From Anamnesis to Diagnosis - A Multimodal Arena for Conversational Clinical Reasoning in LLMs
authors: Federico Ravenda, Mirko Cesarini, Daniele Montagnani, Volodymyr Karpenko, Antonietta Mira, Andrea Raballo
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve expert-level diagnostic accuracy in static evaluations, where the model receives a curated vignette or case report that already condenses the diagnostically relevant findings. Such evaluations measure inference over already selected evidence; the evaluations do not account for the inquiry used to obtain it. In clinical practice, however, diagnosis is an iterative process of inquiry. Clinicians take the patient's history, or anamnesis (Hx), through targeted questioning, examine the patient, and request and interpret tests, progressively narrowing the differential until they reach a final diagnosis (Dx). We introduce Hx2Dx ARENA, an interactive benchmark of 1'000 clinical cases from the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM). Each case is a simulated encounter that proceeds from initial presentation through history taking and physical examination to diagnostic workup. We evaluate open- and closed-source LLMs under multiple configurations. Performance varies considerably across models in the interactive setting, and every model loses diagnostic accuracy relative to the static setting, where the full case is presented upfront. The ability to ask the right questions accounts for much of both the gap between models and the loss of accuracy: diagnosis improves as questions become more targeted and build a more complete clinical picture. LLMs thus reason well once the relevant data are available but remain limited in hypothesis-driven information gathering, in knowing what to ask in order to know. Closing this gap is a prerequisite for their safe integration into real-world diagnostic workflows.

infographic.key_insight: LLMs lose diagnostic accuracy when they must gather information interactively rather than receive a complete case upfront, highlighting limitations in targeted questioning.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Diagnostic accuracy on curated cases may overstate readiness for clinical workflows that require iterative history taking, examination, and test selection.
method: Introduced Hx2Dx ARENA with 1,000 simulated clinical encounters based on NEJM cases.
Evaluated open- and closed-source LLMs under multiple configurations.
Compared interactive information gathering with static, full-case evaluation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Every evaluated model performed worse interactively than with the full case upfront, and more targeted questioning was associated with better diagnosis.
infographic.watch_item: Simulated encounters do not establish real-world clinical safety; hypothesis-driven information gathering remains a key implementation concern.
infographic.paper_title: Hx2Dx: From Anamnesis to Diagnosis - A Multimodal Arena for Conversational Clinical Reasoning in LLMs

title: Applications of Fairness Training in Artificial Intelligence to Ophthalmic Disease Diagnosis using External Eye Photographs
authors: Kostin, V.; Yoon, S.-H.; Chen, J. S.; Baek, S.; Seid, J.; Quyang, N.; Li, E.; Li, E.; Shi, M.; Wang, M.
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR), age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and glaucoma are leading causes of preventable blindness, yet whether external eye photographs carry phenotypic information about posterior segment disease remains unclear, and methods to mitigate demographic disparities in such models are largely unexplored. We developed and evaluated deep learning and vision-language models for binary classification of vision-threatening DR (VTDR), advanced AMD, and glaucoma using 40,687 external eye photographs from 9,878 patients at Massachusetts Eye and Ear. Convolutional networks (WResNet, EfficientNet), a vision transformer (ViT), and a finetuned vision-language model (LLaVA) were assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with fairness across sex, race, and ethnicity quantified by the equity-scaled AUC (ES-AUC). Five fairness-training strategies were applied to the best models. LLaVA achieved the highest baseline AUC for VTDR (85{middle dot}4%, comparable to ViT 82{middle dot}6%); advanced AMD was similar across architectures (EfficientNet 86{middle dot}3%; LLaVA 84{middle dot}8%; ViT 84{middle dot}7%), whereas glaucoma was substantially worse (67-74%). Fairness training improved VTDR and AMD AUCs to 86{middle dot}3% and 85{middle dot}9% while partially mitigating demographic disparities. In summary, although AI models that rely on external eye photography to detect posterior segment disease may not yet be suitable for clinical deployment, the fairness methods demonstrated in this proof-of-concept study could be applied to other AI systems to decrease performance disparities and potentially improve model performance.

infographic.key_insight: AI models detected signals of vision-threatening diabetic retinopathy and advanced AMD in external eye photographs, while fairness training partially reduced demographic performance disparities.
infographic.clinical_relevance: External eye photography may offer a way to study posterior eye disease, but these proof-of-concept models are not yet suitable for clinical deployment.
method: Trained convolutional networks, a vision transformer, and a vision-language model to classify three eye diseases.
Evaluated discrimination using AUC and demographic fairness using equity-scaled AUC across sex, race, and ethnicity.
Applied five fairness-training strategies to the best-performing models.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation used 40,687 photographs from 9,878 patients at Massachusetts Eye and Ear; baseline AUC reached 85.4% for vision-threatening diabetic retinopathy and 86.3% for advanced AMD, versus 67–74% for glaucoma.
infographic.watch_item: Single-center results and only partial disparity reduction leave generalizability and clinical readiness unresolved.
infographic.paper_title: Applications of Fairness Training in Artificial Intelligence to Ophthalmic Disease Diagnosis using External Eye Photographs

title: A Multi-Layered AI Pipeline for BPMN Generation from Natural Language
authors: Alexandru Rancea, Ionut Anghel, Tudor Cioara, Ovidiu Anchidin, Ancuta Nemes
abstract: The automated transformation of unstructured natural language process descriptions into Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) diagrams remains a challenging task, due to linguistic ambiguity and the difficulty to detect non-adjacent control-flow relationships. This paper proposes a solution for generating BPMN models from natural language descriptions through a multi-layered pipeline that integrates transformer-based architectures, Large Language Models and ontology population. The proposed method starts with natural language descriptions and separates textual processing, control-flow relation extraction, and structural validation into dedicated components. Entity extraction is performed using a fine-tuned RoBERTa-based transformer model while a control-flow engine captures non-adjacent relationships through LLM-based inference. To improve generalization under limited available data, the approach uses a dynamic few-shot strategy with con- trolled template input construction, enabling improved generalization under limited data availability. Additionally, an ontology population mechanism is introduced to represent the generated process models as semantic knowledge structures. For evaluation purposes we have used from the literature and industry reference processes. Additionally, we have validated the proposed method on a real-world heart disease patients transitional care process, capturing practical constraints and multi-actor collaboration, and serving as an expert-defined benchmark scenario. Experimental results demonstrate strong performance in the relation extraction task, achieving an accuracy of 90.7%, as well as maintaining structural alignment between the generated and reference BPMN models across multiple evaluation scenarios scenarios.

infographic.key_insight: A multi-layered AI pipeline converts natural-language process descriptions into BPMN diagrams, achieving 90.7% accuracy in control-flow relation extraction.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support documentation of multi-actor care workflows, illustrated by a heart disease transitional care scenario rather than clinical outcome testing.
method: Fine-tuned RoBERTa extracts process entities from text.
LLM inference with dynamic few-shot examples identifies non-adjacent control-flow relationships.
Dedicated structural validation and ontology population support semantic process representation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation used literature and industry reference processes plus an expert-defined heart disease transitional care scenario, reporting structural alignment with reference BPMN models.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report evaluation sample sizes or clinical outcome benefits, limiting conclusions about healthcare deployment readiness.
infographic.paper_title: A Multi-Layered AI Pipeline for BPMN Generation from Natural Language

title: Constructing and Validating Memorisation Audits for EHR Foundation Models
authors: Inigo Stibbe, Joshua Placidi, Padmanabhan Ramnarayan, A. Aldo Faisal
abstract: Autoregressive electronic health record (EHR) foundation models may disclose training information at inference, yet clinical predictability makes patient-specific memorisation difficult to distinguish from generalisation. We evaluate fixed-window token reconstruction, sensitive-attribute disclosure, and random patient-level canaries in GPT-2-style models trained on MIMIC-IV, across early, best-validation, and final checkpoints. Reconstruction improves with additional context, but training--held-out differences remain small. Trajectory-unique prompts containing limited clinical information produce no excess sensitive disclosure for training patients. In a matched model with random binary patient-level canaries, training-patient label-recovery AUROC increases from 0.512 to 0.549 while held-out recovery remains at chance. An overfit 1,000-patient positive control achieves near-perfect recovery, confirming sensitivity to strong memorisation. These results reveal weak cohort-level memorisation but no reliable patient-level disclosure under the evaluated attacks. They motivate clinically grounded inference-time audits that can detect patient-specific memorisation in existing models without retraining with canaries.

infographic.key_insight: The evaluated EHR models showed weak cohort-level memorisation but no reliable patient-level disclosure under the tested attacks.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Privacy audits must distinguish memorised patient information from predictable clinical patterns when assessing EHR foundation models.
method: Evaluated GPT-2-style models trained on MIMIC-IV at early, best-validation, and final checkpoints.
Tested token reconstruction, sensitive-attribute disclosure, and random patient-level canary recovery.
Used an overfit 1,000-patient model as a positive control for strong memorisation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Training-patient canary-recovery AUROC rose from 0.512 to 0.549 while held-out recovery stayed at chance; the overfit positive control achieved near-perfect recovery.
infographic.watch_item: Failure to detect reliable disclosure under these attacks does not establish privacy safety against other attacks or deployment conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Constructing and Validating Memorisation Audits for EHR Foundation Models

title: Do Large Language Models Show Racial and Sex Bias in Pain Management? A Counterfactual Audit of GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, DeepSeek and Qwen
authors: Richard J. Young, Alice M. Matthews
abstract: Racial and ethnic minority patients receive less pain treatment than non-Hispanic White patients, and large language models (LLMs) used as medical AI could reproduce that bias. Prior audits tested a few proprietary models, stated race explicitly and rarely measured the models' own response instability. In exploratory, non-preregistered analyses, Study 1 had four open-weight LLMs assess six acute-pain vignettes in every combination of four races and two sexes, with identity stated or cued only by a name (two names per group), comparing each identity with a White male reference on the same case and sampling seed. In Study 2, 24 configurations of 17 models, including OpenAI's GPT-4.1 mini and gpt-oss, Anthropic's Claude Haiku 4.5, Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash, Meta's Llama, DeepSeek and Qwen, with reasoning on and off and at two precisions, answered the same vignettes and the 50 clinician-written Q-Pain cases. In this single-prompt, JSON-constrained task, no difference survived correction in Study 1, none of 1,386 comparisons survived the false discovery rate in Study 2, and every pain-severity difference was equivalent to zero within one point on a 0-10 scale (within a quarter point for 237 of 238 Q-Pain comparisons). Opioid decisions were bounded less precisely (Study 1 could not exclude differences of about 20 percentage points), so they show no detected difference, not proof of none. The few differences surviving correction within a model favoured Black patients. Models differed far more from one another and across their own settings than between patients (the reference patient received the high opioid dose in 6% to 93% of responses), although serving software, provider and prompt format also differed. Fairness audits of clinical AI should use several names per group, pair comparisons on the seed, report the noise floor and test each deployed configuration.

infographic.key_insight: This audit found no robust racial or sex differences in pain recommendations, while variation across models and settings was much larger.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Clinical AI fairness assessments should test each deployed configuration because aggregate findings may obscure substantial differences in treatment recommendations.
method: Study 1 tested four open-weight LLMs on six acute-pain vignettes, varying race, sex and explicit versus name-cued identity.
Identity comparisons were paired with a White male reference using the same case and sampling seed.
Study 2 evaluated 24 configurations of 17 models on the same vignettes and 50 clinician-written Q-Pain cases.
infographic.evidence_signal: No Study 2 comparison survived false-discovery-rate correction across 1,386 tests; all pain-severity differences met equivalence bounds of ±1 point on a 0–10 scale.
infographic.watch_item: These exploratory, single-prompt results do not establish absence of bias: opioid estimates were less precise, and Study 1 could not exclude differences of about 20 percentage points.
infographic.paper_title: Do Large Language Models Show Racial and Sex Bias in Pain Management? A Counterfactual Audit of GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, DeepSeek and Qwen

title: Agentic Pipeline for Large-Scale Clinical Data Queries in Enterprise Electronic Health Records
authors: Pawar, K.; Tavabi, N.; Kalepalli, A.; Kalepalli, N.; Blackmon, M.; Williamson, A.; Kiapour, A.
abstract: Using electronic health record (EHR) data to answer clinical research questions is challenging. It requires understanding the research question, finding relevant information across different sources, and combining that information to produce meaningful results. We developed an agentic large language model (LLM) pipeline that decomposes investigator-authored requests into source-specific tasks, generates and executes SQL on EHR, integrates structured and unstructured EHR evidence, and applies study-specific clinical note adjudication. We evaluated this workflow against data analyst-identified cohorts across 50 pediatric orthopedic clinical data query requests. Of these, 43 were included in manual-review-adjusted performance analyses. The median adjusted positive predictive value, sensitivity among patients identified by either approach, and corresponding F1 score were 0.93 (95% CI, 0.88-0.98), 0.92 (95% CI, 0.90-0.95) and 0.90 (95% CI, 0.87-0.94), respectively. These findings support the feasibility of translating natural-language research intent into executable, autonomous multi-stage EHR workflows.

infographic.key_insight: An agentic LLM pipeline translated natural-language research requests into multi-stage EHR queries, achieving a median adjusted F1 score of 0.90.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could help researchers identify study cohorts using both structured EHR data and clinical notes.
method: Decompose investigator requests into source-specific tasks.
Generate and execute SQL queries against EHR data.
Integrate structured and unstructured evidence with study-specific clinical note adjudication.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated against analyst-identified cohorts for 50 pediatric orthopedic requests, with 43 included in manual-review-adjusted analyses: median PPV 0.93, sensitivity among patients identified by either approach 0.92, and F1 0.90.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation was limited to pediatric orthopedic requests, and sensitivity was measured only among patients identified by either approach, leaving jointly missed patients unaccounted for.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic Pipeline for Large-Scale Clinical Data Queries in Enterprise Electronic Health Records

title: A Tumour-Aware Multimodal Framework for Explainable Prediction of IDH Mutation in Gliomas from Multi-Sequence MRI
authors: Tahsien Al-Quraishi, Waseem Alwan Zaboon, O. S. Albahri, Raza Nowrozy
abstract: Accurate prediction of isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation status is essential for glioma diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning. Although recent deep learning approaches have demonstrated promising performance, many rely on whole-brain feature extraction and provide limited interpretability. This study proposes a tumour-aware multimodal framework for explainable, non-invasive prediction of IDH mutation status from multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The proposed framework integrates four MRI sequences (T1, T1CE, T2, and FLAIR), tumour subregion segmentation, quantitative radiomic descriptors, and clinical information within a unified deep learning architecture. An ablation study was conducted to evaluate the contribution of tumour-aware learning, radiomic features, and clinical variables. Model performance was assessed using multiple complementary evaluation metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, balanced accuracy, receiver operating characteristic analysis, confusion matrix evaluation, and Grad-CAM visualisation. Experimental results demonstrated that the proposed multimodal framework consistently outperformed the baseline MRI-only model, with the Clinical Fusion model achieving the strongest overall predictive performance. The integration of tumour-aware learning, radiomic descriptors, and clinical information progressively improved classification performance, while Grad-CAM visualisations indicated that the model predominantly focused on biologically relevant tumour regions. These findings suggest that tumour-aware multimodal feature integration enables accurate, interpretable, and non-invasive molecular profiling of gliomas and provides a promising foundation for future clinical decision support in precision neuro-oncology.

infographic.key_insight: A tumour-aware AI framework combining MRI, radiomic features, and clinical information outperformed an MRI-only baseline for predicting glioma IDH mutation status.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support non-invasive molecular assessment of gliomas, but clinical use requires further validation.
method: Integrates T1, T1CE, T2, and FLAIR MRI sequences.
Combines tumour subregion segmentation, radiomic descriptors, and clinical information.
Uses Grad-CAM to visualise regions influencing predictions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Ablation studies and multiple classification metrics favoured the Clinical Fusion model, but the abstract reports no sample size or numerical performance estimates.
infographic.watch_item: External validation is not described in the abstract, leaving generalisability across centres and MRI protocols uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: A Tumour-Aware Multimodal Framework for Explainable Prediction of IDH Mutation in Gliomas from Multi-Sequence MRI

title: Benchmarking Large Language AI Models Against Human Doctors Using an Emergency Medicine Simulation Approach
authors: Shahabian, M.; Hadizadeh Esfahani, A.; Ahmadi, M.; Rajabzadeh, S.; Givechin Ghamsari, M. H.; Tabaraee, A.; Hejripour Rafsanjani, S. Z.
abstract: BackgroundProper adoption of AI in emergency medicine necessitate thorough and rigorous appraisal. Classic benchmarks, which rely heavily on basic question-and-answer formats, though dominating the benchmarking field of LLM usage in medicine, have proven inadequate in assessing the full spectrum of skills incumbent upon an agent in healthcare. MethodsWe propose an intricate benchmarking scheme in which the skill set required of an emergency physician is tested and quantified. Our benchmarking structure is 3-fold: skills such as history taking, diagnostic accuracy, treatment plan, and empathy are evaluated by an emergency medicine expert, while the same expertise is scored by an intern from the perspective of a patient, through what we call a simulated emergency room visit. A comprehensive written examination is also utilized to measure general emergency medicine knowledge. ResultsEight LLMs were benchmarked against each other and in contrast to nine emergency medical doctors. Our findings indicate that the AI models significantly outperformed human physicians across several key domains, including history taking, investigation, diagnostic accuracy, and treatment planning. Furthermore, the models demonstrated superior performance in comprehensibility, credibility, and empathy. When comparing AI models against each other, performance advantages were marginal during simulated emergency room visits and were mostly pronounced during the written examination. ConclusionAI models demonstrate a clear advantage over human physicians across a diverse range of emergency medicine competencies. The proposed benchmarking scheme provides a comprehensive metric for a thorough evaluation of medical skill set, furthering validation, adaptation, and utilization of AI in emergency medicine.

infographic.key_insight: In simulated emergency-room visits, eight LLMs outperformed nine emergency physicians across several evaluated clinical and communication domains.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Simulation results suggest potential for AI support in emergency medicine, but do not establish safety or effectiveness in real patient care.
method: Compared eight LLMs with nine emergency physicians.
Used simulated emergency-room visits scored by an emergency medicine expert and an intern acting as a patient.
Tested general emergency medicine knowledge with a written examination.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports statistically significant AI advantages in history taking, investigation, diagnostic accuracy, treatment planning, comprehensibility, credibility, and empathy, but provides no effect sizes.
infographic.watch_item: The small, simulation-based comparison requires validation in real-world emergency care before clinical deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Benchmarking Large Language AI Models Against Human Doctors Using an Emergency Medicine Simulation Approach

title: PADSNet: Physics-Aware Dual-Stream Network with Biomechanical Priors for Laryngeal Lesion Classification
authors: Zhenzhen You, Weifeng Yu, Zhenghao Shi, Shuangli Du, Minghua Zhao, Yingcheng Zhao
abstract: Precise classification of laryngeal lesions is clinically crucial yet highly challenging, as inter-class visual differences are often subtle. While abnormalities in vocal fold vibratory dynamics provide complementary discriminative information, existing deep learning models predominantly rely on visual appearance and lack explicit mechanisms for modeling clinically meaningful vibratory dynamics. To address this, we propose PADSNet, a Physics-Aware Dual-Stream Network for laryngeal lesion classification that integrates visual representations with explicit biomechanical reasoning. Specifically, a Wavelet-Attention Enhancement Module (WAEM) is designed to bridge the spectral-semantic gap, enabling complementary learning of spatial texture and dynamic frequency representations. Meanwhile, a Knowledge Computing Module (KCM) extracts interpretable biomechanical indices from temporal glottal distance waveforms, including indicators of mobility, symmetry, glottal closure, and vibration stability. These descriptors are subsequently incorporated into a Physics-Aware Gating Module (PAGM) as biomechanical priors to adaptively recalibrate visual feature toward pathology-relevant vibratory patterns. Extensive experiments on a clinical dataset demonstrate that PADSNet achieves an accuracy of 0.8452, an F1-score of 0.8090, a sensitivity of 0.7953, and a specificity of 0.8866. These results indicate that explicitly integrating biomechanical priors with deep visual representations provides a more accurate, robust, and clinically interpretable framework for automated laryngeal lesion classification.

infographic.key_insight: PADSNet combines visual features with explicit vocal-fold biomechanics to classify laryngeal lesions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Vocal-fold motion may provide complementary clues when lesion types have subtle visual differences.
method: Wavelet attention combines spatial texture and dynamic frequency representations.
A knowledge module extracts mobility, symmetry, glottal closure, and vibration stability indices.
Physics-aware gating uses these biomechanical priors to recalibrate visual features.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on a clinical dataset reported 84.52% accuracy, 80.90% F1-score, 79.53% sensitivity, and 88.66% specificity.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report dataset size or external validation, leaving generalizability uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: PADSNet: Physics-Aware Dual-Stream Network with Biomechanical Priors for Laryngeal Lesion Classification

title: Causally Constrained and Uncertainty-Aware Cardiopulmonary Risk Prediction
authors: Yuxiang Lai, Jiashuo Zhang, Liang Zhao, Xiaofeng Yang
abstract: Routine chest computed tomography (CT) captures pulmonary, cardiac, and vascular phenotypes that jointly stratify lung cancer and cardiovascular disease, the two leading causes of death in lung-screening populations. Yet clinical risk calculators evaluate each disease in isolation and omit CT findings, whereas unconstrained machine learning overfits small hospital cohorts, learns treatment- and illness-confounded risk directions, and conceals uncertainty when patient records are incomplete. Here we present the Causal Envelope Agent (CE-Agent), a two-stage framework that compiles peer-reviewed epidemiological evidence into explicit constraints on risk-factor weights before any outcome is seen, while estimating local baseline risk and newly added CT phenotypes from cohort data. At deployment, closed-form uncertainty propagation accounts for missing clinical or CT inputs within milliseconds per patient, running over two orders of magnitude faster than Monte Carlo sampling and returning calibrated risk intervals that direct chart review and selective imaging to borderline patients. Across 53,452 lung-screening participants from 33 US hospitals and 6,814 multi-ethnic adults, CE-Agent outperforms cardiovascular calculators in lung screening, exceeds the Pooled Cohort Equations on hard atherosclerotic events while correcting their 1.7-fold risk overestimation, and generalizes from a single hospital or CT scanner to external sites while lowering required sample sizes up to fivefold. Applied unchanged to lung cancer, CE-Agent matches established screening models with accurate calibration even when restricted to risk-factor directions alone, and pairing both predictions improves joint cardiopulmonary triage from a single screening visit.

infographic.key_insight: CE-Agent combines evidence-based risk constraints with CT findings to predict cardiovascular and lung cancer risk while quantifying uncertainty from missing inputs.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could support joint cardiopulmonary risk assessment from a lung-screening visit and flag uncertain cases for further review.
method: Constrains risk-factor weights using published epidemiological evidence before fitting patient outcomes.
Learns local baseline risk and added CT phenotype contributions from cohort data.
Uses closed-form uncertainty propagation to estimate risk intervals when inputs are missing.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 53,452 lung-screening participants from 33 US hospitals and 6,814 multi-ethnic adults, the abstract reports improved cardiovascular prediction, external-site generalization, and lung cancer performance matching established screening models.
infographic.watch_item: Prospective evaluation is needed to establish whether uncertainty-guided review and imaging improve patient outcomes in routine care.
infographic.paper_title: Causally Constrained and Uncertainty-Aware Cardiopulmonary Risk Prediction

title: Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation: Differentiable Length Control for Concise Clinical Reasoning in Smaller Language Models
authors: Tanzeel Abbas, Ahmad Kamran Malik, Nafees Qamar, Sana Liaqat
abstract: Smaller language models (SLMs) make it feasible to deploy clinical natural language processing where large proprietary models are too costly, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning allows them to be specialised on commodity hardware. One obstacle persists after training: on medical tasks these models answer at far greater length than the clinical question requires. In clinical decision support and point-of-care use, where time is short, such verbosity is hard to act on even when the underlying reasoning is sound. Existing length-control methods depend on preference optimisation, reward models, or proprietary teachers that undercut the accessibility making SLMs attractive. We introduce Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation (PECA), which adds a single differentiable conciseness term to the QLoRA supervised fine-tuning objective. Because the token count is discrete and non-differentiable, PECA instead raises the end-of-sequence probability once generation exceeds a token budget, a smooth signal optimised during ordinary training, with no preference data, no auxiliary model, and a single commodity GPU. On a 1.7-billion-parameter model fine-tuned on the medical-o1-reasoning-SFT corpus, PECA reduces mean response length by 72.8% while improving multiple-choice diagnostic accuracy from 40.8% to 44.0%. A sweep over the conciseness strength traces an interpretable accuracy-to-length frontier for balancing brevity and diagnostic completeness.

infographic.key_insight: PECA reduced mean response length by 72.8% while increasing multiple-choice diagnostic accuracy from 40.8% to 44.0% in a 1.7-billion-parameter language model.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Shorter medical responses could ease review in time-constrained workflows, but clinical usefulness and safety remain unestablished.
method: Adds a differentiable conciseness term to QLoRA supervised fine-tuning.
Encourages end-of-sequence prediction once generation exceeds a token budget.
Requires no preference data or auxiliary model and trains on a single commodity GPU.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports fine-tuning on medical-o1-reasoning-SFT and multiple-choice diagnostic evaluation, with a conciseness-strength sweep showing an accuracy–length trade-off.
infographic.watch_item: Multiple-choice accuracy does not establish whether shorter responses preserve safety-critical details in real clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation: Differentiable Length Control for Concise Clinical Reasoning in Smaller Language Models

title: The BRIDGE dataset: paired brightfield whole-slide images of prostate core-needle biopsies in paraffin, after deparaffinization and H&E staining
authors: Julia A. Mielcarz, Justyna Durślewicz, Marek Zdrenka, Ahmad Abbadi, Martin Eklund, Mateusz Matusiak
abstract: Computational approaches are increasingly being explored to streamline histopathology workflows, including label-free methods that aim to reduce reliance on chemical staining. Among these, deep learning-based label-free virtual staining uses images of unstained tissue to computationally generate stained images. Despite growing interest, model development and validation remain constrained by the scarcity of paired, clinically annotated whole-slide imaging datasets. We present BRIDGE, a dataset of prostate core-needle biopsies collected at the Prof. Franciszek Lukaszczyk Oncology Centre in Bydgoszcz, Poland. The dataset comprises 869 glass slides from 169 patients, each digitized sequentially after sectioning, deparaffinization, and hematoxylin and eosin staining, yielding in total 2607 whole-slide images. The dataset supports the development and external validation of label-free virtual staining, virtual unstaining, image-registration and segmentation methods. Each slide is accompanied by a Gleason score, enabling downstream analyses of cancer classification and grading concordance. The stained images can be used independently for color normalization and cross-scanner robustness studies. All images are de-identified, distributed in their native scanner format and will be available through the BioImage Archive.

infographic.key_insight: BRIDGE provides paired prostate biopsy whole-slide images across three preparation stages to support label-free virtual staining research.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The dataset enables research on computational staining and prostate cancer grading concordance, but does not establish clinical readiness.
method: Sequentially scan each slide in paraffin, after deparaffinization, and after H&E staining.
Pair images across preparation stages for virtual staining, registration, and segmentation research.
Include a Gleason score for each slide to support classification and grading analyses.
infographic.evidence_signal: The dataset contains 2,607 whole-slide images from 869 slides belonging to 169 patients at one Polish oncology centre; the abstract reports no model performance results.
infographic.watch_item: Single-centre sourcing may limit generalizability; clinical use would require independent validation.
infographic.paper_title: The BRIDGE dataset: paired brightfield whole-slide images of prostate core-needle biopsies in paraffin, after deparaffinization and H&E staining
